etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Latin collāpsus (past participle of collābor).

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To break apart and fall down suddenly; to cave in.

quote.citation: 1843, Samuel Maunder, The Scientific and Literary Treasury:
quote.text: A balloon collapses when the gas escapes from it.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To cease to function due to a sudden breakdown; to fail suddenly and completely.
(transitive, computing) In a hierarchical list (such as a directory tree or table of contents), to hide the subentries of (an entry).
(intransitive, cricket) To suffer a batting collapse.

quote.citation: 2023 August 9, Paul Clifton, “Network News: Family-friendly travel: new standard covers pushchairs”, in RAIL, number 989, page 26:
quote.text: Thomas added: "We presented our experiences of frantically trying to collapse a pram, surrounded by loads of grumpy commuters.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To pass out and fall to the floor or ground, as from exhaustion or other illness; to faint.

quote.citation: 2012 April 21, Jonathan Jurejko, “Newcastle 3-0 Stoke”, in BBC Sport‎[1]:
quote.text: The top six are assured of continental competition and after making a statement of intent against Stoke, it would take a dramatic collapse for Newcastle to surrender their place.

quote.citation: 2021 May 5, Paul Clifton, “Network News: Heathrow Western Rail Access scheme 'on hold'”, in RAIL, number 930, page 26:
quote.text: However the collapse in demand for rail and air travel caused by the pandemic has had a knock-on effect for the project's funding.

definitions.definition: Constant function, one-valued function (in automata theory) (in particular application causing a reset). (Can we add an example for this sense?)
